pitch_detail.notes: A ramp of mixed ground that climbs to a tree, which serves as the end of the pitch.
A long snow ramp leading to the foot of a rocky couloir. Gear is almost nonexistent over roughly 55 m, so a slip here is serious.
The mixed crux, up the rocky couloir. It can feel harder or easier with conditions and has a fine alpine atmosphere.
Ice climbing up to where a steeper wall of ice begins.
Keep heading toward the final pillar, which now looms ahead.
The last pillar, about 50 m of steep, clean vertical ice on a full-length rope pitch.

review.changed: Wrote six pitches with the grades given. Left out rappel table: only a general description of abalakovs, horns and old slings is given, with no station list.

pitch_detail.notes: Go up the slab on the right below the headwall, slinging bushes and using thin rock gear that is questionable. You can belay here, or traverse left along the ramp and simul-climb to skip the rope drag.
Traverse left on rock gear, adding short screws in the ice if conditions allow. The belay is on pitons at the end of the traverse, a few metres right of the ice corner where the real ice begins.
Steep ice. For the first 10 m only short screws may bite, though some rock gear exists off to the right. Roughly 50-60 m.
Another full pitch of steep ice of about 50-60 m.

The two upper pitches, each around 50-60 m. The upper third lets you go left or right: left is the easier choice and right is harder. The penultimate pitch usually holds the crux, and taking a direct line there can push into WI6+ territory.

review.changed: Wrote the five entries the source covers for a six-pitch route (pitches 5 and 6 are described together). No lengths where only a range was given. No rappel table: no station list.
review.other_findings: Source says the route ranges WI5 to 6+ depending on line; stored grade WI5+ is consistent.

pitch_detail.notes: An approach pitch of easy ice, about 30-40 m of WI4, then a long snow and ice gully for another 100 m or more. Often one long simul-climbing stretch to the foot of the main dihedral. Belay on screws on the left.

Start up ice on the left toward the dagger guarding the dihedral, then cross right on rock to ice blobs below it. Mixed moves behind the dagger on poor rock with two or three bolts depending on ice, then onto ice in the dihedral. Screw belay with little shelter.

Good ice in the corner. If the corner is dry, drift left up the ice on slabby ground toward an imposing dagger-hung dihedral. Screw belay where the slab meets the headwall; sheltered stances are rare.
Ice up to the corner, then a steep, tiring crux with two bolts on the hardest moves. It eases above, with two more bolts through mixed ground to a ledge with a bolted anchor.
Slabby ground. Head up, then cut a long way left to a second solid ledge, where a bolted belay waits.

Clip two pins and a bolt, then work a long leftward line on horizontal cracks until you hit ice. In lean seasons the ice is delicate daggers with three bolts; in fat years it can form a column. Continue to the trees.

review.changed: Wrote all six pitches with stated grades and lengths. No rappel table: the source says rappel La Pomme d'or and gives no stations.
review.other_findings: Descent: source says the best way down is rappelling La Pomme d'or about 200 m left of the top.

pitch_detail.notes: First of three similar ice pitches of about 140 ft.
Moderate ice of about 140 ft.
Moderate ice of about 140 ft.
Short and steeper at about 80 ft. At the top, traverse the ledge left to a separate gully.
Two choices: ice of about 170 ft, or a mixed variation of about 200 ft that is loose and poorly protected.
A long ice pitch of about 200 ft that stretches a standard rope.
Another rope-length ice pitch of about 200 ft.
Ice pitch of about 200 ft, again nearly the full length of the rope.
Easy ground to the ridge, about 200 ft.

review.changed: Wrote nine pitches with grades and lengths (feet converted). Notes are thin because the source gives little beyond grade and length.
review.other_findings: Descent: climbers right once on the ridge.

pitch_detail.notes: Steps of thin ice in a corner that faces left. The belay is a pin to the left of the first ledge.
A brief, skinny ice step beside a fixed pin leads into another corner of ice.
The last of the ice, ending at a roof formed from a pair of big boulders. Edge leftward on small holds, then reach the snowfield and sling a block for the belay.
Follow the snowfield up to the ridge, with a few easy mixed steps.

review.changed: Wrote all four pitches; the source gives no per-pitch grades or lengths.

pitch_detail.notes: Reach the large ledge by one of three ways: the first pitch of Golden Spike on the left, the easy pitch Ricochet Rabbit on the right, or the ice pillar just left of it. Belay far left at the Golden Spike station, which has one fixed piton.

Two options. Traverse right on thin mixed ground with almost no protection to the pillar, or pass beneath the pillar and squeeze up the ice flow below the roof (easier, about WI5 M4). Either way, clip the fixed pin under the roof, climb the pillar, and finish rightward to a solid ledge belay.
Chimney climbing, starting with more ice and ending in a wider, steep mixed section.
Scramble up mixed steps and a snowy couloir to the ridgeline.

review.changed: Wrote four pitches. Pitch 2 is graded for the harder pillar option; the easier option is in the notes. No rappel table: route is descended by walking.

pitch_detail.notes: Two lines. The right side is steep but with plenty of steps, ending at a sheltered ledge belay on a slung tree about 150 ft up. The left side is steeper and often thinner, with a screw belay in an icy cave about 180 ft up.

From the right-hand belay, continue up the right to a 45 ft column among cauliflower ice; a pin anchor above lets you rappel, while another curtain higher leads to a pin or screw station beside the frozen pool. From the left-hand belay, traverse right 15-20 ft and climb the steep pillar. If descending by rope, move right and downclimb briefly to that pin station.
A 50 ft section that can be soloed or roped, reaching the gully above. To walk off, follow the drainage a bit farther, then gain the ridgeline directly east.

review.changed: Wrote three pitches; pitch 1 grade left out because the two options are graded differently (WI4+ right, WI5 left). Lengths left out where two options differ. No rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb the blocks left of the corner to a 16 ft pillar leaning on the wall. Go up either side of the pillar on face holds, then belay.
Follow cracks to a spot beneath a giant corner, then cross slab to a ledge for the belay.
Slab up to a left-leaning ramp, then follow the ramp to a ledge.
Flakes lead rightward to a corner that faces and arcs to the right.
Climb the right-facing, right-arching corner until you reach the snow bench.
The crux. Take the dihedral on the bench's left side, clipping the pin that is second in the pitch. Move right and go straight through the overhang, then cut left near the top to a ledge.
Simple climbing to the top of the wall.

review.changed: Wrote all seven pitches. Gear sizes and bolt counts not stated per pitch.
review.other_findings: Source says the original grade was 11b but the stated 5.11+ is consistent with the stored grade.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb into the chimney system. Start with a short face section just right of a small right-facing dihedral (about 5.7-5.8) or go a little left for a 5.4 way in. Climb the chimney to the big ledge spanning much of the face.

Shift the belay east to the far end of the ledge, below a left-facing dihedral. Climb the dihedral and the crack system above it for a long way to a good ledge. Graded 5.6, though some find it closer to 5.7.
Several crack systems and dihedrals leave the ledge, with no obvious best choice. After a short steep section the terrain eases; aim for the right side of the summit tower base and a good ledge.
A short pitch up cracks facing east, ending on a large ledge on that side.
A very short east-to-west traverse along the foot of the summit tower, ending near the southwest arete beneath the wide final crack. Some topos link it with the previous pitch.

The famous finish. The wide crack is better avoided as an offwidth; take the thin crack and face to the right. The crux bulge needs a stay-left, reach-high move to a small face hold, with a pin below the move but none above. Then traverse right and up to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote six entries covering seven pitches (pitches 1 and 2 are described together). No rappel table: descent is described but not as a station list.
review.other_findings: Source describes seven pitches while the row stores six. No length is stated.

pitch_detail.notes: Go up and gently left among many cracks and flakes, with some loose rock and scattered pins that may mislead. Do not follow the large flake to the right with footholds, since that forces a 5.8+ downclimbing traverse left. Belay options are many; an old pin sits on a ledge around 130-140 ft up.

Moderate ground with at least four pins confirming the way. Belay on a comfortable ledge about 100 ft up beside a large right-facing flake, or use the historic alcove up and left with pins on its back wall.

Loose moderate ground with a long horizontal crack for gear, to the famous piton ladder of four or five pins on delicate face climbing, sometimes wet. Watch for rope drag. Above the last pin, either traverse left round an arete (harder) or a few feet right to flakes and cracks to Lunch Ledge.
Move the belay left along Lunch Ledge to its far left end, below steeper dihedrals.

Pick a line left of the large wet dihedral, then back right into it, or stay one dihedral left for harder starting moves. The original line traversed left partway up to finish on Alexander's Chimney. A full rope of about 195 ft reaches a ledge with marginal gear, or belay lower for better protection.

Several dihedrals lead on to Broadway; the far right is wet and wide. A small clean dihedral two to the left of the large wet one is dry and enjoyable. A full rope gets you to Broadway, topping out left of the exposed move at the ledge.

review.changed: Wrote six pitches matching the stored count. Grades only where stated. No rappel table: the rappels described belong to a different line and are not station by station.

pitch_detail.notes: Work up to a surprising crack running to a roof, then angle up to a ledge on the right. Climb a blank face for about 20 ft to a faint crack system, follow intermittent cracks to the roof base, saving a #3 cam for the wide crack under it. Stop and belay, or carry on up and right to the tree ledge using a double-length runner.

Grubby trees, then a right-facing corner to a ledge. Behind the trees find a right-angling crack to a long narrow roof; traverse right 20 ft and pull the roof where it narrows, watching rope drag. After the roof come 5.6 moves with no protection. Can link with pitch 3 on a 70 m rope.
A ramp leading left to the base of a right-facing dihedral.

Corner and a brief steep crack lead to a ledge; from there go up-left to a short cracked headwall. Pull the vertical bit avoiding loose rock, repeat on the second headwall. Can link with pitch 5 on a 70 m rope.
Mostly a scramble: follow the ridge through a chimney to a grassy ledge. The belay is amid loose rock beneath the next dihedral.
Climb a right-facing dihedral and turn the roof at its top, to a belay ledge below a steep wall.
Straight up the crack, graded 5.10a, though the hard section is very short and protects well. The alternative hand-traverses right from the crack to a ledge, said to be about 5.9.
Climb the pillar's right flank where it leans, cross a small roof, then run the rope out to a spot where you can unrope and rack up.

review.changed: Wrote all eight pitches. Pitch 7 grade given as the guidebook figure the text quotes. No rappel table: route is descended by walking.
review.other_findings: Pitch 7 is quoted at 5.10a, above the stored route grade of 5.9; the 5.9 variation is the alternative.

pitch_detail.notes: Right-facing corners and a twin crack lead to a little ledge that has one bolt.
Keep following the corner, then moderate patina face climbing to a stance with two bolts. Pitches 1 and 2 can be linked.
Step right and undercling past a flake to enter a different crack system in a shallow corner. Build a natural-gear belay on small ledges higher up.
Very rotten, crumbly rock to the top; many parties stop and rappel after pitch 2 or 3 instead.

review.changed: Wrote four pitches. No rappel table: no stations listed.

pitch_detail.notes: Same as the first pitch of the neighbouring classic: two bolts and mid-size gear up to a pair of anchor bolts under the large boulder.

Go up and left around the boulder on very secure ground with optional small to medium gear, to a crumbly chimney. A few jamming moves, exit left, being careful not to pull rock off. A few more moves to a shoulder-high ledge for a gear anchor.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches. No rappel table: descent given as a short downclimb then rappels, not a station list.

pitch_detail.notes: Follow the left-leaning ramp of the easy neighbouring route for two pitches, about 300 ft, to the higher juniper on Lower Juniper Ledge. Long slings reduce drag. A 70 m rope reaches the lower tree with some simul-climbing. The old tree belay is gone; a bolt and a tied-off horn remain.

From the second tree go up the ramp a short way to a left-facing dihedral, climb it passing a replaced bolt to its top, then pull left onto a poor-rock ledge to a diagonal crack. Work left and clip another new bolt, then to under the big roof. The belay sits in a comfortable notch with good gear.

Climb steep rock on jugs, trending right to the roof, then follow the base of the roof rightward. Go through the roof just left of or below a small tree. Belays are poor on the final slab, so many link up to the high ridge with about 40 ft of simul-climbing on a 70 m rope.

review.changed: Wrote three entries covering the five stored pitches (1-2 and 4-5 are described together).
review.other_findings: Pitch 3 is stated as 5.10c; stored grade is 5.10.

pitch_detail.notes: Start on a boulder right of the neighbouring route. Follow the right-facing corner for around 20 ft, then step across to a left-facing one and take it past a bolt to a belay ledge.
Step right, then angle back up and leftward along a crack to finish on top of the formation.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches; no grades or lengths in source.

pitch_detail.notes: A hand-to-offwidth crack with good stemming rests. Multiple hard spots appear where footholds vanish or wide pods call for real effort, and a last wide section leads to a ledge.
Broken crack systems with good jams and many face holds. Traverse right when possible and finish up the squeeze chimney.
Straight up rambly crack systems with some face climbing and good gear, through a dirty chute trending left to a dirty alcove.

Loose and not well cleaned. Traverse sketchy dirt to the crack start, clip a bolt, and pull a loose-ish jug block. Continue up the open-book cracks on good gear with one short runout, pass the first roof, then the large roof crux to a small ledge.
Not recommended: finish the dihedral through loose rock with surprisingly good gear and top out on a scree slope, which showers the belayer. A two-bolt rappel anchor is on the cliff above the slope.

review.changed: Wrote five pitches. No rappel table: only a general descent description is given.

pitch_detail.notes: Low-angle ledgy climbing on good rock with minimal gear.
Traverse about 5 m left from the anchor, then up a crack on good gear. Continue up and left, passing the big tree, to an anchor on the right edge of a gully.
Climb the scree slope or gully to the hand crack, a very fine splitter, then through two small ledges to the anchor.
Up and left past a single move, then the scree slope to a tree belay with a dyneema sling.

review.changed: Wrote four pitches. No rappel table: only that the route can be rapped with one 70 m rope.
review.other_findings: Pitch 3 to 2 is a rope-stretcher on a 70 m rope.

pitch_detail.notes: Traverse up and left, then up the face. An emergency rappel station is at bolt 4, so climb past it.
A technical face on good holds, finishing past a small overhang.
Easy start, then pull through a roof.
Up and left, clipping the first bolt and continuing on easy but loose ground.
A few easy moves lead to an improbable-looking face with plenty of holds. Semi-hanging belay.
A short right-facing flake then easier ground.
Gentle terrain with just two bolts, ending on a wide ledge.
A technical face with crimps, slopers, flaring cracks and hard clips, past a natural arch to a ledge.
Up and right on good jugs, then back left on a technical face. Hanging belay.
Technical face with crimps, underclings and poor footholds. Semi-hanging belay on a small ledge.

The crux. Three bolts, then a thin traverse up and left into a huge flaring groove, out on a thin face past a pocket to a thin left-hand flake that should be treated gently. The third bolt only protects the belayer and may be unclipped.
Low-angle ground reaches a two-bolt station near 35 m; a further 25 m, with one more bolt, ends at a tree. Watch for loose rock. Can be split at the station.

review.changed: Wrote all twelve pitches. No rappel table: descent is a hike, rappelling not recommended.

pitch_detail.notes: Traverse up and right, then easy blocky rock.
Good rock ending at a small stance.
More easy, good rock.
Traverse right across the gully, follow the bolt line on the green gully's right side, then recross to a stance on the left.
Easy limestone to a ledge below a large wavy overhang.
Climb up and right over rock waves past a rappel station into a long sequence of moves on superb rock.

Two ways exist: either head directly rightward, or after the first clip downclimb right and go straight at bolt two. Both involve crimping sharp holds, then easier ground to the ledge below a big overhang.
Traverse up and right on rock that looks suspect but is good, then a steep solid face to a friction traverse, and right up an easy flake to a stance.
Back left on positive holds, then a few powerful layback moves on a vertical rail to a small exposed ledge.
Crimpy face past a hollow flake to a rest ledge, then easier ground through a bottleneck. Keep right for better rock.
Easy, well-bolted finishing pitch. Take care with loose blocks at the top.

review.changed: Wrote all eleven pitches. No rappel table: descent is a hike.

skip_reasons.co_palisades_the_great_chimney: No per-pitch text: the account is a trip narrative, not pitch-by-pitch beta.
